skills.name: Factorise by a common factor and by grouping

note.text:
Factorising is the reverse of expanding: write the expression as a product.
• Common factor: find the highest common factor (HCF) of all the terms, numbers and letters, and take it outside a bracket: 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3); 4x² − 10x = 2x(2x − 5).
• Check by expanding: the bracket must give back the original expression.
• Fully factorised: nothing more can be taken out of the bracket.
• Grouping (four terms): factorise pairs, then take out the common bracket: ax + ay + bx + by = a(x + y) + b(x + y) = (a + b)(x + y).

sections.heading: Factorising undoes expanding
sections.text:
Expanding turns a product into a sum: {bracket(3, [2, 'x'], [5, ''])} = {poly([6, 'x'], [15, ''])}.
Factorising goes back: from {poly([6, 'x'], [15, ''])} we find {bracket(3, [2, 'x'], [5, ''])}.
Step one is the highest common factor (HCF) of all the terms. {3} divides both {6} and {15}, and nothing bigger does. Write the HCF outside, and inside the bracket write each term divided by it.
Always check by expanding your answer: you must get the original expression back.

sections.heading: Letters can be common factors
sections.text:
Look at the letters as well as the numbers. In {poly([8, 'x²'], [12, 'x'])}:
• numbers: the HCF of {8} and {12} is {4};
• letters: x² = x × x, so x is in both terms.
The HCF is {mono(4, 'x')}, so {poly([8, 'x²'], [12, 'x'])} = {mono(4, 'x') + '(' + poly([2, 'x'], [3, '']) + ')'}.
If you take out only {4} or only x, the answer is factorised but not fully factorised: something common is still inside.

sections.heading: Four terms: grouping
sections.text:
Sometimes no factor is common to all four terms, as in {poly([1, 'x²'], [3, 'x'], [2, 'x'], [6, ''])}.
Group the terms in pairs and factorise each pair: x{'(' + poly([1, 'x'], [3, '']) + ')'} + {2}{'(' + poly([1, 'x'], [3, '']) + ')'}.
Now the bracket {'(' + poly([1, 'x'], [3, '']) + ')'} is common, so take it out: {'(' + poly([1, 'x'], [3, '']) + ')' + '(' + poly([1, 'x'], [2, '']) + ')'}.

key_words.meaning: write as a product of factors
a number or expression that divides exactly
highest common factor: the biggest factor shared by all the terms
no common factor is left inside the bracket

mistake.why: The first answer is not fully factorised: x is still common to both terms in the bracket.

steps: HCF of the numbers {g * m} and {g * n} is {g}.
Both terms contain x, so x is common too: the HCF is {mono(g, 'x')}.

Check by expanding: that gives {mono(-a - b, 'x')}, but the expression has {mono(a + b, 'x')}.

solution: Take out the common bracket {'(' + poly([1, 'x'], [a, '']) + ')'}: the answer is {answer}.

misconceptions.explain: Not fully factorised: the bracket still has a common factor. Take out the highest common factor, {k}.
x is only in one term, so it cannot be taken out.

solution: The HCF of {k * m} and {k * n} is {k}.
{k * m} ÷ {k} = {m} and {k * n} ÷ {k} = {n}, so the answer is {answer}.

questions.prompt: {poly([k * m, 'x'], [k * n, 'y'])} = k(…). What is the number k taken out (the highest common factor)?

misconceptions.explain: {k * m * n} is too big: it does not divide {k * m}.

solution: The HCF of {k * m} and {k * n} is {k}: {k * m} = {k} × {m} and {k * n} = {k} × {n}.
